If you take Sarkeesian for example, the whole controversy over online harassment surrounding her Kickstarter campaign generated over 25 times what she originally was looking for and so she basically used those funds to turn FF into a full-fledged not-for-profit organization.

I think the phrase 'professional victim' is less black-and-white than most people who use it seem to believe, but it's still clear nonetheless that without drumming up emphasis on the harassment she received, that wouldn't have happened. (Not going to get into the entire issue of people in these positions faking harassment against themselves, operating on good faith and just assuming all of the harassment was in fact legit.)

Now, that organization basically focuses on education and developing critical content, which is totally fair. Organizations are allowed to do whatever they want to do, and take whatever stance they want to take. However, FF tends to be take views that most people find infuriatingly ridiculous (she recently went out of her way to criticize the newly-announced Doom game for being violent, for example). Naturally, specifically calling out one of video gaming's most famous franchises (which is a sci-fi horror shooter) for being violent is silly. It's not a meaningful criticism to say "this game is too violent and that's disturbing"; it's a personal preference at best, but here basically is a thinly veiled way of saying "anyone who likes this is a lesser person than I am."

So, of course, when things like this rub people the wrong way, there's a response that keeps her and her organization in the news: people write articles, they tweet, news outlets pick up on it, etc. And, of course, a percentage of those people who go out of the way to respond will engage in some kind of harassment, which then itself becomes something else to fuel coverage.

The trick here is that there's a blurry line between a 'professional victim' and someone who's just professionally controversial. It's not like she's the first person to ever operate this way. The 'victim' phrase is probably just because she, and people who operate similarly to her, also go out of their way to present themselves as sympathetic by pointing attention to the harassment they receive. Most people who are the victims of internet harassment (which is a weird area to begin with, the legal definition is pretty loose there) can pretty easily avoid it if they find it so troubling. This also fuels the disdain for people like her, they will take openly controversial stances which are likely to make them targets of mean tweets and whatnot, and then discount the fact that their stance was likely to incite the response. Which is distinct from saying "she's asking for it", it's more like having enough social skills and common sense to understand that if I walk into an Italian restaurant and start complaining that I don't like Italian food out loud, people are likely to tell me to go somewhere else. It would be disingenuous in that situation to then claim some kind of harassment because I'm being excluded from the restaurant at that point.

It's not about just defining people you don't like as 'professional victims'. Most people find anyone that's professionally controversial as off-putting, especially when they make themselves virtually unavoidable in the context of their hobbies/passions. If someone really loves video games, but one out of ten or twenty articles on their favorite gaming site is about some new non-controversy, they're inclined to just get frustrated with it and not act rationally.
